DONE (s470bq, Opus, 2026-09-05).  docs/generated-cl-ir-review.md Â§3.2 (now
CLOSED there); ir-spec Â§1 and Â§11b reader rule 5 rewritten.

CL string syntax has no `\n` escape, so `print "fib: $n\n"` used to emit a
literal containing an ACTUAL newline: a grep hit half a string, a diff split
literals across hunks, line counts stopped matching form counts.  Now a literal
holding any character below 0x20 goes out as `(p-esc "â¦")`, whose payload
spells those characters with the DATA FORM's escape alphabet (`\\ \" \n \t \r
\uXXXX`, ir-spec Â§12b) -- deliberately the same alphabet, so a backend
implements ONE unescape for `--emit-sexp` and for `p-esc`.

`p-esc` is a MACRO that decodes at macroexpansion, so the compiled code holds
the same constant string and the run is unchanged; an unknown escape in the
payload is an ERROR naming it (a silently-copied bad escape would be a wrong
STRING, i.e. a value the program consumes).

EMITTED ONLY WHEN NEEDED: no control character, no wrapper -- which is what
keeps the flag-day's diff explainable file by file.  Non-ASCII does NOT
trigger it (the file stays readable).

THREE SITES WERE ROUTED THROUGH THE ONE WRITER to get it, which is a rule-11
win on its own: heredocs (their body is the corpus's densest source of
newlines) and `__DATA__` had their own inline escapers, and both therefore
lacked #419's unrepresentable-code-point split as well.

THE ONE EXCEPTION, and it is deliberate: `p-let`'s `:perl` fact and `p-sub`'s
`:prototype` sit inside a plist the macro READS as a literal list, so a
`(p-esc â¦)` there would be a two-element sublist where a consumer expects a
string.  Those two slots take `Pl::ExprToCL::cl_string_datum`, which never
wraps -- named so the exception is visible at the call site.
